summary: Long-tail p95/p99 latency spikes due to continuous batch window growth on short, bursty requests
description:
Issue summary: Starting 2026-03-12 09:10 UTC, NoteStream reported recurring high tail latency (p95/p99) and intermittent request timeouts for short, single-turn text-generation calls. The spikes present as long-tail latency increases without corresponding CPU/GPU saturation, and are concentrated on a small percentage of requests during periods of low-to-moderate QPS with bursty microbursts.

Impact: Customers using the dedicated pool (NoteStream) are observing 5–10% of requests hitting p95/p99 spikes up to 3–4x baseline, causing frontend timeouts and user-facing slowdowns. There are business-impacting errors for NoteStream's editors flow (timeouts at 8s).

Environment: Dedicated pool in prod:us-east (d-htx-a cluster), model variants: redwood-mini-v1 and a quantized llama-2-13b variant. Autoscaling configured with min 2, target 8 gpus. Batching mode: continuous batching enabled with default max_batch_delay=20ms; adaptive window growth enabled.

Observed behavior: During short bursts (spikes of 10–50 concurrent single-token or short-prompt requests), the scheduler appears to increase batch window to coalesce small requests; however measured batch wait times for the affected batches jump to 60–120ms in the p99, and some requests subsequently hit application-level timeouts at 8s due to head-of-line waiting through multiple batches. Throughput and GPU utilization remain healthy overall.

Expected behavior: Continuous batching should maintain low per-request wait time for short requests by constraining max_batch_delay or capping adaptive-window growth; p95/p99 should remain close to baseline under low-to-moderate QPS.

Temporary workaround suggested to customer: Switch to fixed strict batching profile (max_batch_delay=5ms) or disable adaptive-window growth for their dedicated pool, which reduces observed p99s to near baseline in canary tests.
steps_to_reproduce: 1) Use dedicated pool with continuous batching enabled (default config).
2) Send many short single-turn requests in microbursts (10–50 qps bursts, 10–30s duration).
3) Observe p95/p99 for end-to-end request latency (client->response) rising during bursts even though GPU utilization remains under 60%.
4) Toggle batching to strict (max_batch_delay=5ms) and repeat; p99 drops significantly in our tests.
logs: 2026-03-12T09:12:03.112Z scheduler[pid=2134] INFO batch_id=9876 wait_ms=72 size=6 policy=adaptive_window
Tracing: https://traces.redwood.ai/trace/abc123 (shows multiple consecutive batch-queue spans)
investigation_notes: 2026-03-12 10:00 UTC - Initial triage by Support (Aisha): collected traces, customer timing, and config; reproduced on staging with dedicated pool replica.

2026-03-12 11:10 UTC - SRE (Diego) reproduced tail latency in canary; isolated to continuous/adaptive batching path where window growth allowed successive small batches to accumulate head-of-line requests.

Hypothesis A: Adaptive window growth is over-aggressive for workloads with short, bursty requests; the algorithm increases delay to hit amortized throughput targets, increasing tail latency for those requests.

Hypothesis B: KV-cache warmup interacts with batch coalescing: first-context requests cause longer kernel selection / mem-copy latencies that cascade into subsequent batched requests under the same time window.

Mitigation tests: reducing max_batch_delay to 5ms and disabling adaptive growth reduced p99 by ~65% in canary. Increasing min throughput per-batch (min_batch_size=2) reduced head-of-line waiting but increased overall latency for tiny requests—tradeoff noted.

Next actions: (1) Recommend customer apply temporary config change to strict batching; (2) engineering to add telemetry for per-batch 'adaptive-window' growth events and correlate with tail latencies; (3) evaluate quick patch to cap window growth per-tenant.

Engineering to deliver telemetry and a cap-on-growth patch (tracked in INT-1287). Follow-up scheduled with NoteStream for 2026-03-14 to validate changes.
